title: What Happened to the British Sitcom?
standfirst: A golden age, a long decline, and a few signs of life.

readingList.title: Laughing Matters: A History of Television Comedy
In Defence of the Long Novel

body: For a few decades, Britain made some of the best situation comedies in the world. Whole families sat down together to watch them, and their catchphrases passed into everyday speech. Ask most people to name a great sitcom from the last ten years and they will struggle.

The classic British sitcom was simple. A small cast, a fixed setting, and characters trapped by their own flaws. Viewers knew the people and laughed because they recognised them. The jokes came from character, not from shock.
Crucially, these shows were watched by almost everyone at the same time. With only a few channels, a hit comedy became a shared national experience, talked about at work the next morning.

Audiences split across hundreds of channels and then across streaming services. Broadcasters became more cautious, and fewer new comedies were given the time to find their feet. Many of the old favourites took a series or two to become great. Today, a show that does not succeed at once is often cancelled.
Tastes changed too. The fashion moved towards comedies with no studio audience, filmed like dramas. Some were brilliant. Few became the kind of shared joke that the old shows had been.

There is still an appetite for warm, character-led comedy, as the steady repeats of old favourites show. Some of the most promising new work is being made online, by small teams who answer to their audience rather than to a commissioning editor. The format is not dead. It may simply have moved.
